doc.title: Jay Leonhart interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Bucky Pizzarelli's rhythm guitar technique
summary: Leonhart explains that Bucky plays only one or two notes in the chord with a Freddie Green style chunk, unlike young guitarists who play too many notes.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: Yeah. I just, to me there’s nothing like that chunking — what do they call it — hollow body —
That Freddie Green rhythm. Well Bucky’s a master of that.

Yeah. And it’s also the notes he puts on top of the chord, too. I’ve noticed, in fact I wanted to talk about Milt Hinton a little, he was on a Dick Hyman record that I just think is great. And it wasn’t just the chunking, it was the note as it moved on the top of the chord [scats], you know that voice leading.

Well you know, I’ll tell you a little secret. Most of the time there’s one note in the chord. Most of the time Bucky’s doing, he’s dampening most of the notes and playing one, the third or the seventh [scats]. You listen carefully. There’s not six notes, five notes, there’s not even three notes. At best there’s two notes. Two notes coming through and the rest of it is chunk, chunk, chunk, chunk. And you get that sensational combination of a drum [scats]. He is the simplest guy. And that’s why he can play any song at all. He doesn’t have to know all the upper partials of it. When there’s a solo playing he’ll play all the upper partials of it. But when he’s playing rhythm guitar, and that’s the key to it, that’s why it sounds so good, because it’s not notey and full of — and that’s what rhythm guitar players today, young guys who will pick up a Martin steel string and start playing rhythm guitar on it, they’re trying to play all the notes and they don’t understand it doesn’t sound good.

See, yeah, blang, blang, blang, and it takes too long for the [scats] for all those notes to — with Bucky it’s [scats], it’s really just two little notes. Always. Always. That’s his key. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -15-
